fields.title: Plast: Forty Requirements from One Person
fields.summary: You have a list of requirements, a single highly persistent stakeholder, and a one-quarter deadline. Decide where to start to avoid repeating the previous failed rollout.
fields.decisionPrompt: Where will you start working on the product?
fields.brief/role: You are an internal product manager at Plast.
fields.brief/company: Plast is a fictional plastic packaging manufacturer: three workshops, 400 people, 120 pieces of equipment.
fields.brief/context: You have been tasked with building an internal product for equipment repair requests. The head of maintenance sent a document with forty items, marking all of them as urgent. Two years ago, the company tried to implement a similar system—it failed to take off, and everyone went back to using a spreadsheet. You have one quarter for the first version, after which the budget will be reviewed.
fields.brief/objective: Deliver a version that people will actually start using within a quarter, rather than a version that ticks off all forty items.
fields.brief/constraints: Two developers and you. No designer. A quarter is about 22 person-weeks of work. The developers estimate that the forty items will take a year.
fields.brief/task: Decide where you will start and explain the reasoning behind your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A list of requests is not requirements
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A document with forty items, all marked urgent, tells you about its author, not the product. Before estimating such a list, ask two questions: who else can block this, and what is the product actually being compared to? The answer almost always changes both the requirements and the roadmap—and a slice that covers the entire user journey end-to-end turns out to be half the size of the top ten 'most important' items.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Forty items, all marked 'urgent'. The phrasing is mostly like this:

'Request creation button on the home screen', 'Filter by workshop', 'Excel export', 'Telegram notifications', 'Color-coded priority', 'Mobile version', 'Integration with 1C', 'History for each machine', 'Print work order', 'Dashboard for management'...

At the end of the document, there is a note: 'All of this was already in the system we looked at two years ago.'

Not a single item explains why it is needed or what will change if it is not built.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
The head of maintenance is the author of the document. He writes every day; his influence on the decision is medium since he does not control the budget.

Operations Director—signs off on the budget and decides whether to extend the project after the quarter. He has attended only one meeting in two months and does not dive into details. The only thing he mentioned out loud was: 'I need to understand how much equipment downtime we have.'

Mechanics (14 people)—those who will create and close requests. None of them have attended meetings: they are in the workshops, while the meetings are in the office.

Occupational Safety Department—during the previous rollout, they demanded at the last minute that work orders for hazardous work be printed with a physical signature, which stalled the project for a month. No one has spoken to them this time yet.

Accounting accepts invoices for outsourced repairs and has nothing to do with the product.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
A request is created like this: a mechanic calls or writes in a general chat, the head of maintenance adds a row to the spreadsheet, prints the work order, and marks it as completed after the repair.

The spreadsheet has been in use for three years, contains 4000 rows, and everyone knows how to use it. Nobody complains about the spreadsheet itself—they complain that 'it is unclear what is currently in progress' and 'equipment is down, but we only find out after the fact.'

Regarding the previous rollout, the head of maintenance says: 'It had everything, but to submit a request, you had to fill out fourteen fields. The mechanics just kept calling.'

Off-the-shelf systems exist on the market, starting at 800 thousand per year, and cover almost the entire forty-item document.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
From the developers:

'Forty items will take a year if done properly. Within a quarter, we can realistically build an end-to-end flow: create a request, see it in the list, assign it, and close it. Plus maybe one extra feature on top.

What scares us: half of the items are phrased as interface elements. We will build exactly what is written, and then it will turn out that something else was needed.

Specifically: printing a work order takes two days. 1C integration takes three weeks, and you cannot do it halfway.'

The Operations Director expects a demo at the end of the quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Map stakeholders and build an end-to-end slice
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: One week: talk to the mechanics and occupational safety, map the forty items to user journey steps, assemble the thinnest slice that covers the entire end-to-end flow, and write acceptance criteria for it.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
A week is spent on conversations. In the workshop, you find out that mechanics do not want to submit requests themselves—they want to still be able to call, with the request appearing automatically. Occupational safety states their requirement immediately: work orders for hazardous work must be printed with a signature, otherwise they will block the rollout.
The forty items are mapped to the steps 'request → assignment → work → closure' and condensed into a slice of nine items. The remaining thirty-one move to the second and third rows of the map.
By the end of the quarter, the end-to-end flow works, work order printing is available, and mechanics can call—the head of maintenance creates the request, just like before. All 14 mechanics and both shifts are using it.
At the demo, the Operations Director asks about equipment downtime; there is no direct figure, but there is data from which it can be calculated in two days.
Compromise: you spent one week out of thirteen on conversations and consciously skipped thirty-one out of forty items.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Take the first ten items and start building
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The document already exists, and the author is right there. Sort the forty items by importance with him, take the top ten, and hand them over to development this week.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Development starts immediately. Over the quarter, ten items are built: filters, color-coding, export, dashboard, and machine history.
You cannot use this: closing a request did not make it into the top ten because it seemed obvious and was twelfth on the list. Requests are created but hang indefinitely.
A week before the demo, occupational safety appears demanding printed work orders with signatures. Printing takes two days, but the requirement comes with a question about why no one spoke to them.
At the demo, the Operations Director sees a dashboard with no data. The project is extended for a quarter 'for finishing touches'.
Compromise: you moved fast from day one and ended up with a set of features that do not form a working process.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: An off-the-shelf solution covers almost the entire document and costs less than a year of development. Propose the purchase to the Operations Director and redirect the team to other tasks.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The calculation looks convincing, and the director agrees to take a look. Three weeks later, there is a demo: the system covers 34 out of 40 items.
At the meeting, the head of maintenance reminds everyone that they bought a similar one two years ago and it failed because of the fourteen fields in the request form. The question of how this off-the-shelf system is different remains unanswered: you compared feature lists rather than how requests are actually created.
The purchase is postponed. The quarter is wasted, the product has not started, and returning to it is now harder due to lower trust.
Compromise: you compared yourself to a third-party product by checkboxes and failed to compare either to how people actually work today.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Write acceptance criteria for all forty items
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The main issue with the document is its vagueness. Spend two to three weeks turning every item into a verifiable condition so the team does not build the wrong thing.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Three weeks are spent on rewriting. The document becomes noticeably better: 'convenient filter' turns into verifiable conditions, and almost no controversial phrasing remains.
Then the unpleasant truth emerges: forty well-described items still require a year of work, and the quarter is now three weeks shorter. The priority has not changed because acceptance criteria do not affect it.
In the end, you still have to cut scope, but now in a rush and without talking to the mechanics.
Compromise: you resolved a real problem—ambiguity—but spent time on it that should have been used to figure out what to build first.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Requirements were gathered from the loudest person, not from everyone who can block the project
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A stakeholder with high influence and low interest was ignored until the very end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The current way of working is not considered as the primary alternative
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A request was mistaken for a task: the phrasing lacks a verifiable 'so that'
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Scope was cut based on importance rather than user journey coherence
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: 'Done' was not defined by a verifiable condition before starting work
